newsitem.title: INDIA: China's 96/97 sugar purchases set to rise - expert.
newsitem.headline: China's 96/97 sugar purchases set to rise - expert.

text.p: China's sugar purchases in the new season beginning in October could go up substantially after a dip in 1995/96, a senior industry official said on Thursday.
"I suspect next year China will return to imports," Guy Toller, director of London-based C. Czarnikow Sugar Ltd, told the Asia International Sugar Conference held in the Indian capital.
Toller said it was difficult to predict how much China would buy since its imports would depend on bilateral agreements with Cuba.
"We do anticipate a return to the market by China next year. Their import requirements would also depend on how their bilateral agreement with Cuba goes," Toller said.
Toller said China may require somewhere between 1.2 and 2.2 million tonnes in 1996/97.
He said China bought only small quantities of sugar in 1995/96. He did not give any details.
Toller said the domestic market in China was beginning to pick up, a signal that stock levels had started falling.
He said the world surplus built up during 1995/96 could be bigger than it appeared as there were surplus stocks in India, much of which had not been exported.
India is expected to produce a record 16.5 million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96, sharply up from 14.6 in the previous season.
By end September India is likely to have a carry forward stock of 8.0 million tonnes of sugar against a statutory requirement of 3.0 million, after exports of one million tonnes.

"The real supply/demand result in the market place is therefore much closer to balance and correlates with world prices that have remained about 12.00 cents per pound basis spot raws for the past year," Toller said.
He said world prices had remained at these levels because the supplies, though available, had not actually hit the world market and been sitting in India.
Peter Baron, executive director of the International Sugar Organisation, said physical presence of big quantities would have an effect on prices.

Toller said despite good crops in Thailand, Australia, Brazil and South Africa, in the new season a slight reduction in production in India was expected and output in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries was under pressure.
"The potential numbers are unbelievable," he said.
He said Coke was outselling Pepsi by three-to-one across China and had increased its share of the growing Chinese soft drink market from 18 percent last year to 23 percent this year.
Advertising spending to drive home recognition of the brand into the minds of China's consumers is basically doubling each year, but Farrell declined to give any figures.
He said the biggest problem the company faced was finding and training suitable staff fast enough to keep up with the explosive growth rate.
